short: The peace agreement that established the enduring modern borders of Scandinavia.
full:
Signed on 27 May 1660, the Treaty of Copenhagen concluded the Second Northern War between Sweden and Denmark-Norway. Driven by the unexpected death of Charles X Gustav and the successful Danish defense of Copenhagen, the treaty rolled back some of the harshest Swedish demands previously imposed at Roskilde. While Sweden retained the rich southern provinces of Scania, Halland, and Blekinge, it was forced to return the island of Bornholm and the Norwegian province of Trøndelag.

This settlement proved remarkably durable, establishing the geographical boundaries between Sweden, Norway, and Denmark that largely exist today. It recognized a balance of power in the Baltic, ensuring that no single nation exercised absolute dominance over the Sound, a key strategic objective enforced by the mediating naval powers of the Dutch Republic, England, and France.
